title: Why Don't Birds Get Shocked on Power Lines?

lines.text: This bird is standing on thousands of volts.
Touch that wire from the ground, and it could kill you instantly.
So why is the bird fine?
But electricity only flows when there's a difference in pressure between two points, like water flowing downhill.
Both feet grip the same wire, at almost exactly the same voltage.
The current stays in the metal, a far easier path than a bird's body.
But if a wing touches a second wire, or a grounded part of the pole, the bird completes a circuit.
Now the current goes right through it.
That's why small birds are safe, and big birds aren't.
An eagle's wings can stretch nearly two meters, wide enough to bridge the gap.
Power lines are one of the biggest human-made dangers to eagles.
So bird-safe poles space the wires farther apart, and cover the dangerous parts.
The bird isn't immune to electricity.
It just never gives it anywhere to go.

sources: Avian Power Line Interaction Committee (APLIC), Suggested Practices for Avian Protection on Power Lines (2006): eagle-safe designs use ~60 in (1.5 m) horizontal phase separation, insulating covers and perch management.
Loss, Will & Marra (2014), Refining estimates of bird collision and electrocution mortality at power lines in the United States, PLOS ONE.
US Fish & Wildlife Service: electrocution on power poles is a major human-caused source of golden and bald eagle mortality.
Golden and bald eagle wingspans are roughly 1.8-2.3 m (Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds).
Distribution lines birds commonly perch on run at roughly 4-35 kV; current flows only through a path with a potential difference across it.
